title: Chapter 44 — The Chart
paragraphs: If you had followed Captain Ahab down into his cabin after the squall that took place the night after that wild ratification of his purpose with the crew, you would have seen him go to a locker in the stern, bring out a large wrinkled roll of yellowish sea charts, and spread them before him on his bolted-down table. Then, sitting down before them, you would have seen him intently studying the various lines and shadings that met his eye, and with slow but steady pencil tracing additional courses over spaces that had been blank before. At intervals he would refer to stacks of old log-books beside him, in which were set down the seasons and places where, on various past voyages of various ships, sperm whales had been captured or seen.

While he worked this way, the heavy pewter lamp suspended in chains overhead rocked constantly with the ship's motion, throwing shifting gleams and shadows of lines across his wrinkled brow. It almost seemed that while he himself was marking out lines and courses on the wrinkled charts, some invisible pencil was also tracing lines and courses upon the deeply marked chart of his forehead.

But it was not only on this particular night that Ahab pondered over his charts alone in his cabin. Almost every night they were brought out. Almost every night some pencil marks were erased and others substituted. For with the charts of all four oceans spread before him, Ahab was threading a maze of currents and eddies, all with a view to the more certain accomplishment of that monomaniac thought of his soul.

Now, to anyone not fully acquainted with the ways of the leviathans, it might seem an absurdly hopeless task to seek out one solitary creature in the boundless oceans of this planet. But not so to Ahab. He knew the patterns of all tides and currents. By calculating the drifting of the sperm whale's food, and by recalling the regular, established seasons for hunting him in particular latitudes, he could arrive at reasonable estimates — almost approaching certainty — about the most timely day to be on this or that ground in search of his prey.

So well established, in fact, is the sperm whale's periodic return to given waters that many hunters believe that, if he could be closely observed and studied throughout the world — if the logs for a single voyage of the entire whale fleet were carefully compared — then the migrations of the sperm whale would be found as unvarying as those of the herring shoals or the flights of swallows. On this hint, attempts have been made to construct elaborate migratory charts of the sperm whale.*

*Since I wrote the above, the statement has been happily confirmed by an official circular issued by Lieutenant Maury of the National Observatory, Washington, on April 16th, 1851. That circular shows that exactly such a chart is now being completed, and parts of it are presented in the circular. "This chart divides the ocean into districts of five degrees of latitude by five degrees of longitude; perpendicularly through each of which districts are twelve columns for the twelve months; and horizontally through each of which districts are three lines; one to show the number of days that have been spent in each month in every district, and the two others to show the number of days in which whales, sperm or right, have been seen."

Besides, when making a passage from one feeding-ground to another, the sperm whales — guided by some infallible instinct, or rather, let us say, by secret intelligence from the Deity — mostly swim in what are called veins. They continue their way along a given ocean-line with such undeviating exactness that no ship ever sailed her course, by any chart, with one tenth of such marvelous precision. In these cases the direction taken by any one whale may be as straight as a surveyor's parallel, and his line of advance may be strictly confined to its own unavoidable, straight wake; yet the arbitrary vein in which he is said to swim at these times generally takes in some few miles of width (more or less, as the vein is presumed to expand or contract), but never more than can be swept by the eye from the whale-ship's mastheads as she glides cautiously along this magic zone. The upshot is that at particular seasons, within that breadth and along that path, migrating whales may be looked for with great confidence.

And so, not only at known times, upon well-known separate feeding-grounds, could Ahab hope to encounter his prey. Even in crossing the widest expanses of water between those grounds, he could, by his skill, so position and time himself along the way as to still have some prospect of a meeting.

There was a circumstance that at first glance seemed to entangle his delirious but still methodical scheme. But perhaps it did not in reality. Though the gregarious sperm whales have their regular seasons for particular grounds, you generally cannot conclude that the herds that haunted such-and-such a latitude or longitude this year, say, will turn out to be identically the same as those found there the season before — though there are peculiar and unquestionable cases where the contrary has proved true. In general, the same remark applies, only within narrower limits, to the solitaries and hermits among the mature, aged sperm whales. So although Moby Dick had in a former year been seen, for example, on what is called the Seychelle ground in the Indian Ocean, or in Volcano Bay on the Japanese coast, it did not follow that if the Pequod visited either of those spots at any later corresponding season, she would infallibly meet him there. The same was true of some other feeding-grounds where he had at times shown himself. But all these seemed only his casual stopping-places and ocean-inns, so to speak, not his places of long residence. And where Ahab's chances of achieving his object have been spoken of so far, the reference has only been to whatever wayside, preliminary, extra prospects were his before a particular fixed time or place was reached — when all possibilities would become probabilities, and, as Ahab fondly thought, every possibility the next thing to a certainty. That particular time and place were joined in the one technical phrase: the Season-on-the-Line (the Line being the equator). For there and then, for several consecutive years, Moby Dick had been periodically sighted, lingering in those waters for a while, just as the sun in its annual round loiters for a predicted interval in any one sign of the Zodiac. It was there, too, that most of the deadly encounters with the white whale had taken place; there the very waves were storied with his deeds; there also was that tragic spot where the monomaniac old man had found the awful motive for his vengeance. But with the cautious thoroughness and unresting vigilance with which Ahab threw his brooding soul into this unfaltering hunt, he would not allow himself to rest all his hopes on the one crowning fact just mentioned, however flattering it might be to those hopes; nor, in the sleeplessness of his vow, could he so calm his unquiet heart as to put off all searching in the meantime.

Now, the Pequod had sailed from Nantucket at the very beginning of the Season-on-the-Line. No possible effort could have enabled her commander to make the great passage southward, round Cape Horn, and then, running down sixty degrees of latitude, arrive in the equatorial Pacific in time to cruise there. Therefore he had to wait for the next season. Yet the premature hour of the Pequod's sailing had perhaps been correctly chosen by Ahab with a view to this very state of things. For an interval of three hundred and sixty-five days and nights lay before him — an interval which, instead of enduring it impatiently ashore, he would spend in a miscellaneous hunt, in case the White Whale, spending his vacation in seas far from his periodical feeding-grounds, should by chance turn up his wrinkled brow off the Persian Gulf, or in the Bengal Bay, or the China Seas, or in any other waters haunted by his race. So Monsoons, Pampas, Nor'-Westers, Harmattans, Trades — any wind but the Levanter and the Simoon — might blow Moby Dick into the devious zigzag world-circle of the Pequod's circumnavigating wake.

But granting all this, if you regard it discreetly and coolly, does it not seem a mad idea — that in the broad, boundless ocean one solitary whale, even if encountered, should be thought capable of being individually recognized by his hunter, like a white-bearded Mufti in the crowded thoroughfares of Constantinople? Yes. For the peculiar snow-white brow of Moby Dick, and his snow-white hump, could not fail to be unmistakable. And haven't I tallied the whale's marks, Ahab would mutter to himself, as, after poring over his charts until long after midnight, he would throw himself back in reverie — tallied him, and shall he escape? His broad fins are bored, and scalloped out like a lost sheep's ear! And here his mad mind would run on in a breathless race, until a weariness and faintness of pondering came over him, and he would seek to recover his strength in the open air of the deck. Ah, God! what trances of torment that man endures who is consumed with one unachieved, revengeful desire. He sleeps with clenched hands, and wakes with his own bloody nails in his palms.

Often, when he was driven from his hammock by exhausting and intolerably vivid dreams of the night — dreams which took up his own intense thoughts of the day and carried them on amid a clash of frenzies, whirling them round and round and round in his blazing brain until the very throbbing of his life-spot became unbearable anguish — and when, as was sometimes the case, these spiritual throes heaved his being up from its foundations, and a chasm seemed to open in him, from which forked flames and lightnings shot up, and accursed fiends beckoned him to leap down among them — when this hell within him yawned beneath him, a wild cry would be heard through the ship, and with glaring eyes Ahab would burst from his stateroom, as though escaping from a bed that was on fire. Yet these outbursts, perhaps, instead of being the irrepressible symptoms of some hidden weakness, or of fright at his own resolve, were only the plainest signs of its intensity. For at such times crazy Ahab, the scheming, unappeasably steadfast hunter of the white whale — this Ahab who had gone to his hammock — was not the agent that made him burst from it again in horror. That agent was the eternal, living principle, or soul, in him; and in sleep, being for the time separated from the characterizing mind, which at other times used it as its outer vehicle or agent, it spontaneously sought to escape from the scorching nearness of the frantic thing of which, for the time, it was no longer an integral part. But since the mind does not exist unless joined with the soul, it must have been that in Ahab's case, as he yielded up all his thoughts and fancies to his one supreme purpose, that purpose, by the sheer stubbornness of its own will, forced itself, against gods and devils, into a kind of self-assumed, independent being of its own. Indeed, it could grimly live and burn while the common vitality to which it was joined fled horror-stricken from the unbidden and unfathered birth. Therefore the tormented spirit that glared out of bodily eyes, when what seemed Ahab rushed from his room, was for the time only an emptied thing, a formless sleepwalking being — a ray of living light, to be sure, but without an object to color, and therefore a blankness in itself. God help you, old man, your thoughts have created a creature in you; and he whose intense thinking thus makes him a Prometheus — a vulture feeds upon that heart forever; that vulture the very creature he creates.
